title: Explaining why a statistical diagram leads to misinterpretation of data
summary: Audit scales, symbols, labels, samples and selected time windows, quantify the distortion, and propose a fairer display.
objectives: Identify visual and contextual features that can distort a statistical diagram.
Quantify exaggeration caused by truncated axes or resized symbols.
Explain how to redraw or annotate a diagram so that it communicates fairly.

sections.title: Audit the scale before trusting the shape

blocks.text: Check where each axis begins, whether tick intervals are equal, whether any break is marked and whether two graphs use comparable scales. A bar graph normally begins at zero because bar length encodes magnitude. A truncated baseline can be legitimate when small changes need detailed study, but it must be conspicuous and the reader should not mistake the displayed height for the full value.

The scores 84 and 92 in the diagram look very different above a baseline of 80. Their displayed heights are 4 and 12, a ratio of 3, although the actual values differ by only 8 and have a ratio close to 1.1.

sections.title: Inspect symbols, labels and missing context

blocks.text: A picture scaled in both width and height represents quantity by area, not by side length. Doubling the side of a square makes its area four times as large; doubling every dimension of a solid makes its volume eight times as large. Decorative three-dimensional bars also introduce perspective, making front objects appear larger than equal objects behind them.

Misinterpretation can also come from missing units, an unclear key, unequal time intervals, sectors that do not total 360°, or selecting only dates that support a claim. A percentage without the original sample size can exaggerate a small change, and an average without its type or data spread may hide important differences.

sections.title: Worked example: quantify a truncated-axis exaggeration

prompt.text: The bar chart in the diagram shows scores 84 and 92 above a baseline of 80. Compare the displayed-height ratio with the actual-value ratio and explain the risk.

content.text: Subtract the baseline to find the visible bar heights.

The graph makes the second score look three times the first in bar height, although it is only about 9.5% greater. Redraw the bars from zero, or keep the break mark and say clearly that the chart shows differences, not full sizes.

sections.verification_note: The arithmetic separates the visual ratio 3 from the data ratio of about 1.095. Drawn from zero, the bars would be 84 and 92 units tall, almost equal.

sections.title: Worked example: detect area distortion

prompt.text: Two square icons represent values 20 and 40. The first has side length 3 cm and the second has side length 6 cm. Explain why the display exaggerates the increase.

content.text: The area appears four times as large for a value that is only twice as large. Use equal-sized repeated symbols, a bar whose length doubles, or square sides scaled by the square root of the value ratio.

sections.verification_note: Equal-sized unit symbols or a zero-based bar graph would show a factor of 2, matching the data instead of the misleading area factor of 4.

sections.title: Explain the effect and propose a repair

blocks.text: A strong critique names the feature, describes the false impression and supports the claim with numbers. ‘The graph is misleading’ is incomplete. A precise explanation might say that the non-zero baseline changes bar heights from 84 and 92 to 4 and 12, making a 9.5% increase look like a threefold comparison.

Then recommend a repair: begin a magnitude-encoding bar chart at zero, use equal intervals, label units and sample sizes, preserve proportional symbol area, show the complete relevant time period and identify missing or estimated values. If a truncated axis is necessary for detailed fluctuation, mark the break and state that the chart focuses on differences rather than full magnitudes.

prompt.text: Values 63 and 66 are drawn above a baseline of 60. By what factor is the second displayed bar height greater than the first?

feedback.text: The displayed heights are 63 − 60 = 3 and 66 − 60 = 6. Their ratio is 6 ÷ 3 = 2, even though 66 is less than 5% more than 63.

blocks.text: Inspect titles, units, baselines, tick intervals, axis breaks, keys, time windows, sample sizes and totals before accepting the visual impression.
Quantify the distortion by comparing displayed lengths or areas with the actual data relationship. Remember that area scales with length squared and volume with length cubed.
State the likely misinterpretation and propose a specific fairer scale, symbol, label set or time window. A critique should connect visual design to mathematical evidence.
